description: Test your knowledge of PA H6 | Aplastic Anemia & Bone Marrow Failure.

cards.text: What are the three diagnostic criteria that must be present to diagnose aplastic anemia?
cards.answer: Pancytopenia (reduced RBC, WBC, platelets) + hypocellular bone marrow + absence of abnormal cells (dysplasia/malignancy), fibrosis, or infiltration.

tip.tip: Think: "Empty marrow" — fat and stroma replace blood cells. The *morphology* differentiates aplasia from MDS or leukemia.

cards.text: Which drug classically causes dose-independent (idiosyncratic) bone marrow suppression in aplastic anemia?
cards.answer: Chloramphenicol — causes both predictable dose-dependent and rare dose-independent marrow suppression; classic example of idiosyncratic aplasia.

tip.tip: Chloramphenicol = idiosyncratic marrow toxin. Other cytotoxic drugs (busulfan, cyclophosphamide) are dose-dependent and predictable.

cards.text: What is the predominant pathogenic mechanism in ~80% of acquired aplastic anemia cases?
cards.answer: Immune-mediated T-cell destruction — activated CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes attack haematopoietic stem cells via Fas-FasL, perforin/granzyme, and cytokine release.

tip.tip: Evidence: patients respond to immunosuppressive therapy (ATG + ciclosporin). Think: self-tolerance breaks down after drug/viral trigger.

cards.text: Name two inherited causes of aplastic anemia and their key distinguishing features.
cards.answer: Fanconi anemia — AR, DNA repair defect, skeletal anomalies (absent thumbs/radii), café-au-lait spots, childhood onset, high leukemia risk. Dyskeratosis congenita — X-linked, telomerase mutation, triad of nail dystrophy/oral leucoplakia/skin pigmentation.

tip.tip: Fanconi = Fanc*y* skeletal defects + leukemia risk. Dyskeratosis = dys*keratin* = skin/nails/mouth findings.

cards.text: What is the clinical presentation triad of aplastic anemia and what symptom corresponds to each lineage failure?
cards.answer: RBC↓ = fatigue/dyspnea/pallor; WBC↓ = recurrent infections; Platelet↓ = petechiae/purpura/mucosal bleeding. Key negative finding: NO hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy.

tip.tip: "3 pancyto" — three lineages fail, three symptom clusters. Absence of organomegaly rules out infiltrative disease or leukemia.

cards.text: How does pure red cell aplasia differ from aplastic anemia?
cards.answer: Pure red cell aplasia = selective destruction of erythroid precursors only (parvovirus B19 typically); produces isolated anemia without thrombocytopenia or neutropenia. Aplastic anemia = all three cell lines reduced.

tip.tip: Pure RCA = parvovirus; single lineage affected. Aplastic = all three lineages; more severe and life-threatening.

cards.text: What is the key diagnostic finding that differentiates aplastic anemia from myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) and leukemia?
cards.answer: Hypocellular marrow with no dysplastic or malignant cells in aplastic anemia; MDS has dysmorphic cells; leukemia has blasts. Marrow *cellularity and morphology*, not pancytopenia alone, make the diagnosis.

tip.tip: Aplasia = empty marrow. MDS = marrow with abnormal morphology. Leukemia = marrow crowded with blasts.

cards.text: Which viral infection classically causes post-hepatitis aplastic anemia, and what type of hepatitis is it?
cards.answer: Non-A, non-B, non-C seronegative hepatitis (hepatitis-associated aplasia) — no identifiable hepatitis virus on serology; aplasia typically occurs 2-3 months post-hepatitis and is often severe.

tip.tip: "Seronegative hepatitis" = mysterious viral trigger. One of the few post-infectious aplasias; requires high suspicion for diagnosis.
